title: How to Deal With Insurance Adjuster After a House Fire
description: Learn how to deal with insurance adjuster after a house fire: what to say, what to document, and how to protect your Galveston fire claim from day one.
keyword: how to deal with insurance adjuster after a house fire
html:
A house fire turns your life upside down in minutes, and within a day or two you will be talking to the insurance company's adjuster. Knowing how to deal with insurance adjuster after a house fire can make a real difference in how complete your claim is. The adjuster is not your enemy, but they work for the insurer, and their estimate is the starting point for everything you are paid. This guide gives Galveston homeowners a practical, step-by-step approach to the first meetings, the inspection, the contents inventory, and the negotiation that follows.

Understand Who the Adjuster Works For

The adjuster assigned to your fire claim may be a staff employee of your insurer or an independent adjuster hired by the insurer. Either way, their job is to evaluate the claim on behalf of the insurance company. Many are fair and professional. But their estimate reflects what they saw, what they chose to include, and the pricing their company uses. You have the right to your own documentation, your own estimate, and your own representation by a public adjuster licensed by the Texas Department of Insurance (TDI).

Before the First Adjuster Meeting

  • Report the claim promptly and write down your claim number and adjuster's name and contact information.
  • Get the fire department report or incident number. The insurer will want it.
  • Request a certified copy of your policy, including declarations and endorsements, so you know your limits for dwelling, other structures, contents, and additional living expenses (ALE).
  • Take your own photos and video of every room, even rooms that look untouched. Smoke and soot travel through HVAC ducts, attics, and wall cavities.
  • Secure the property. Board up openings and tarp the roof if needed, and keep receipts. The policy requires reasonable steps to prevent further damage.
  • Track every expense: hotel, meals above your normal cost, laundry, mileage, pet boarding. These may be covered under ALE.

How to Deal With Insurance Adjuster After a House Fire: The Inspection

The first inspection sets the tone. Use these rules:

  1. Be present and walk every room. Point out smoke odor, soot on ceilings and inside closets and cabinets, heat damage to windows and fixtures, and water damage from firefighting.
  2. Ask what they are including. Will the estimate cover cleaning or replacement of HVAC ducts? Attic insulation? Electrical wiring near the fire? Odor sealing of framing?
  3. Stick to facts. Answer questions honestly and briefly. Do not guess about the cause, timelines, or values. "I don't know" is an acceptable answer.
  4. Take notes. Write down what the adjuster says, especially promises about follow-up, experts, or advances.
  5. Do not sign anything you do not understand. Releases, final settlement forms, and contractor authorizations deserve a careful read.
  6. Ask about an advance. Many insurers will issue an advance on contents or ALE so you can get through the first weeks.

Recorded Statements and Examinations

The insurer may ask for a recorded statement. Your policy likely requires cooperation, but you can ask to schedule it, prepare, and have a representative present. Review your timeline of the day of the fire, stay consistent, and do not speculate about how it started. If the insurer requests an examination under oath, take it seriously and consider getting professional help before it happens.

Smoke Damage Is Often Underestimated

The most common gap in fire estimates is smoke and soot. Fine soot particles settle on surfaces far from the fire and can cause lingering odor and corrosion. A light wipe-down is not the same as proper cleaning, sealing, and in some cases replacement. Watch for:

  • Soot inside cabinets, closets, drawers, and HVAC returns
  • Odor that returns on warm, humid days, which is common on the Gulf Coast
  • Discolored grout, plastics, and metal fixtures
  • Contaminated insulation and ductwork

Our Galveston fire claims page covers smoke and soot issues specific to coastal homes.

Building the Contents Inventory

The contents list is often the largest and most time-consuming part of a fire claim. Insurers typically require a room-by-room inventory with a description, quantity, age, and replacement cost for each item.

  • Go room by room, then drawer by drawer and closet by closet.
  • Use photos, old social media posts, online order history, bank and credit card statements, and receipts to prove ownership and value.
  • Include smoke-damaged items that cannot be cleaned effectively, not just burned items.
  • If your policy pays replacement cost, keep receipts when you replace items so you can recover withheld depreciation.

Reviewing the Adjuster's Estimate

When you receive the estimate, compare it line by line to what you saw. Check:

  • Scope: Did they include every room and every damaged surface?
  • Quantities: Are square footages and linear feet correct?
  • Pricing: Do prices reflect actual Galveston-area labor and material costs?
  • Code upgrades: Rebuilding may trigger current building code requirements. If your policy includes ordinance or law coverage, those costs may be payable. See our Galveston local code page.
  • Depreciation: How much was withheld and what is needed to recover it?

Our claim settlement calculator can help you see how deductible and depreciation affect what you actually receive.

Know the Timelines

Under the Texas Prompt Payment of Claims Act, Insurance Code chapter 542, insurers must meet specific deadlines to acknowledge a claim, request information, accept or reject it, and pay once accepted. Keep a dated log of every communication. If deadlines slip, note it in writing.

Handling Disagreements With the Adjuster

Part of learning how to deal with insurance adjuster after a house fire is knowing what to do when you disagree. Start by identifying the specific line items in dispute rather than rejecting the whole estimate. Send a written list of missing or underpriced items with supporting photos, contractor bids, or cleaning specialist reports. Ask the adjuster to reinspect specific rooms. If the disagreement is about the amount of loss rather than coverage, check whether your policy includes an appraisal clause, which lets each side choose an appraiser to resolve value disputes. If the disagreement is about coverage, ask for the insurer's position in writing, including the policy language it relies on.

Communication Rules That Protect Your Claim

Consistent, documented communication is the backbone of how to deal with insurance adjuster after a house fire.

  • Put important requests and disagreements in email, not just phone calls.
  • Send documents with proof of delivery and keep copies.
  • Be polite and persistent. Frustration is understandable, but stay focused on facts.
  • Do not throw away damaged items until they have been documented and the insurer confirms it does not need to inspect them.
  • Do not accept a "final" payment until you are confident the estimate covers everything.

When to Bring in a Public Adjuster

Some homeowners decide the simplest answer to how to deal with insurance adjuster after a house fire is to let a professional do it. Consider professional help if the estimate seems low, the smoke damage is being minimized, the contents inventory is overwhelming, or the insurer is delaying. A public adjuster represents you, prepares an independent estimate, documents the full scope, and handles the back-and-forth with the insurance adjuster. Outcomes are never guaranteed, but you will not be navigating it alone.

faq.q: Should I talk to the insurance adjuster after a house fire?
faq.a: Yes, you need to cooperate with the insurer. Be present for the inspection, answer honestly and briefly, take notes, and avoid guessing about the cause or values. You can have a public adjuster represent you.

faq.q: Do I have to accept the insurance adjuster's fire damage estimate?
faq.a: No. You can review it line by line, submit your own documentation and estimate, and request a revision. Many policies also include an appraisal process for disputes over the amount of loss.

faq.q: What is often missed in a house fire insurance claim?
faq.a: Smoke and soot damage in areas away from the fire, HVAC and insulation contamination, code upgrade costs, and smoke-damaged contents are commonly underestimated.
